questions.q: What is the rule for creating an equivalent fraction from a given fraction?
questions.a: You must multiply or divide both the numerator and the denominator by the same non-zero whole number. A wrong answer like "adding the same number to the top and bottom" reveals the student confuses multiplication with addition, which changes the value of the fraction entirely.

questions.q: If you have 1/3 of a pizza and your friend has 2/6 of a pizza, who has more? Explain why.
questions.a: They have the same amount. 2/6 is equivalent to 1/3 because multiplying both parts of 1/3 by 2 gives 2/6. A wrong answer suggesting "2/6 is more because the numbers are bigger" shows the student is ignoring the relationship between the numerator and denominator and focusing only on the size of the digits.

questions.q: Find an equivalent fraction for 3/4 that has a denominator of 12.
questions.a: Step 1: Identify that 4 times 3 equals 12. Step 2: Multiply the numerator (3) by the same number (3). Step 3: Result is 9/12. A wrong answer like 6/12 indicates the student identified the denominator change but failed to apply the same operation to the numerator.

questions.q: Is it possible to find an equivalent fraction for 7/11 by multiplying the numerator by 2 and the denominator by 3? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, it is not possible. You must perform the same operation on both to keep the value the same. If you change them differently, you create a new, unrelated fraction.

questions.q: You are given 10/20. Can you simplify this to a fraction with a smaller denominator?
questions.a: Yes, divide both by 10 to get 1/2. A student who says "no" likely does not realize that division is a valid tool for finding equivalent fractions, or they do not see 10 as a common factor.

questions.q: Create two different equivalent fractions for 2/5 and explain how you made them.
questions.a: Acceptable answers include 4/10 (multiplied by 2) and 6/15 (multiplied by 3). A poor answer would be random numbers that don't maintain the ratio, showing they haven't grasped the "same operation" rule.
